```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A model fitted with `s(log(x))` uses a transformed covariate, but we may want
to predict at supplied values of `x`, plot the result against `x`, or estimate
change per unit of `x`. This vignette shows how to make those choices while
keeping the model's transformation intact.

We load {gratia} and {mgcv} for the examples:

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
```

## Fit a count model with a transformed covariate and an effort offset

We simulate independent Poisson counts. The rate per unit of effort varies
nonlinearly with `log(x)`, and multiplying that rate by effort gives each
observation's expected count. Thus, twice the effort gives twice the expected
count at the same value of `x`.

```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(42)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(150, 1, 5), effort = runif(150, 1, 3))
dat$y <- rpois(nrow(dat), dat$effort * exp(sin(log(dat$x))))
```

With a log link, the multiplicative effort term becomes an additive
`offset(log(effort))`. We fit a smooth of `log(x)` to estimate the remaining
variation in the log expected count:

```{r model}
m <- gam(y ~ s(log(x), k = 6) + offset(log(effort)),
  family = poisson(), data = dat, method = "REML")
```

## Predict at values of the original covariates

Supply the original `x` and `effort` values when predicting at new observations;
gratia evaluates their transformations. Here we hold effort at two units and
compare the contribution of the smooth with the complete fitted mean.
`smooth_estimates()` needs only `x`, whereas `fitted_values()` also needs the
effort offset:

```{r raw-data}
nd <- data.frame(x = seq(1.2, 4.8, length.out = 8), effort = 2)
smooth_estimates(m, data = nd["x"])
fitted_values(m, data = nd)
```

Without supplied prediction data, `smooth_estimates()` creates an evenly
spaced grid on the scale used in the smooth: here, `log(x)`. We can plot the
estimated contribution directly on that scale:

```{r coordinates}
sm <- smooth_estimates(m, n = 30)
draw(sm)
```

If you already have values on the transformed scale, supply a column named
exactly as it appears in the model, here `log(x)`:

```{r evaluated-data}
evaluated <- data.frame(`log(x)` = log(nd$x), check.names = FALSE)
smooth_estimates(m, data = evaluated)
```

If both `x` and `log(x)` are supplied, gratia computes the transformation from
`x`. To build a grid on the original scale, use `data_slice()` with the
original fitting data. The following call creates eight evenly spaced `x`
values while holding effort at two:

```{r raw-slice}
data_slice(m, x = evenly(x, n = 8), effort = 2, data = dat)
```

## Plot against the original covariates

Drawing methods use the model's covariate coordinates by default. For example,
`log(x)` is plotted against `log(x)`, with a matching axis label, whether it is
inside a smooth or a parametric term. Set `back_transform = TRUE` to display
`x` instead. The estimated smooth contribution remains on the model's linear
predictor scale. The following calls request an axis in the original units,
first from the fitted model and then from saved smooth estimates.

```{r back-transform}
draw(m, back_transform = TRUE)
sm_raw <- smooth_estimates(m, back_transform = TRUE)
draw(sm_raw, back_transform = TRUE)
```

The same option works for transformed covariates in parametric terms. We fit a
Poisson model with a linear effect of `log(x)` and the same effort offset.
Plot the effect against `log(x)` and `x`, then make the plot in the original
units using the output of `parametric_effects()`.

```{r back-transform-parametric}
m_parametric <- gam(y ~ log(x) + offset(log(effort)),
  family = poisson(), data = dat)
draw(m_parametric)
draw(m_parametric, back_transform = TRUE)
pe <- parametric_effects(m_parametric)
draw(pe, back_transform = TRUE)
```

For a surface, `back_transform = TRUE` changes both displayed axes. To
illustrate this, we add an independent covariate `z` and fit a tensor-product
smooth using `log(x)` and `sqrt(z)`. The simulated counts still depend only on
`x` and effort; `z` supplies a second axis for this display example:

```{r back-transform-surface-data}
dat_surface <- transform(dat, z = runif(nrow(dat), 1, 4))
```

Fit a smooth over the transformed coordinates, then request original-scale
axes for both covariates when drawing it.

```{r back-transform-surface}
m_surface <- gam(y ~ te(log(x), sqrt(z)) + offset(log(effort)), family = poisson(),
  data = dat_surface, method = "REML")
draw(m_surface, back_transform = TRUE, contour = FALSE)
```

`back_transform = TRUE` also changes where a smooth is evaluated when the
grid is generated automatically. For example, consider `s(log(x))` with `x`
ranging from 1 to 100. By default, three equally spaced points on the log scale
correspond to 1, 10 and 100 in the original units. With
`smooth_estimates(..., back_transform = TRUE)`, the same grid size gives 1,
50.5 and 100 in the original units. The smooth is evaluated at the logs of
these values. `draw(m, back_transform = TRUE)` prepares this grid automatically.

Precomputed estimates retain their chosen evaluation points. An object created
on a transformed-only grid cannot be drawn on the original scale: its raw
coordinates are unavailable. Recompute it with `back_transform = TRUE`, or
supply original covariate values through `data` when calculating the estimates.

### Use your own transformation functions

The transformation need not be named `log()` or `sqrt()`. Each smooth axis
must depend on one distinct original model covariate, and the transformation
must be available when calculating predictions. Here `foo()` is another name
for `sqrt()`; we supply its environment through `envir`:

```{r back-transform-alias}
foo <- sqrt
m_foo <- gam(y ~ s(foo(x), k = 6), family = poisson(), data = dat)
sm_foo <- smooth_estimates(m_foo, back_transform = TRUE, envir = environment())
draw(sm_foo, back_transform = TRUE)
```

Keep the original fitting data and transformation functions available when
creating automatic original-scale grids. If the fitting data are unavailable,
supply prediction rows in `data`; if a function or constant is missing, supply
its environment in `envir`. Saved estimates can then be plotted without
evaluating the transformation again. Rugs and partial residuals require the
original observations and are omitted when those observations cannot be
recovered.

Soap-film boundary coordinates are stored on the model scale. A transformed
boundary has no retained raw coordinates, so raw-scale drawing raises an
error. Draw these soap films with `back_transform = FALSE` to retain their
boundaries.

The old `parametric_effects(transform = ...)` argument is deprecated. Replace
`transform = TRUE` with `back_transform = FALSE`, and `transform = FALSE` with
`back_transform = TRUE`.

## Preserve functions defined inside a model-fitting function

A fitted model may retain the formula expression without retaining the local
environment in which it was evaluated. In the example below,
`transform_x()` needs the local constant `shift`. We return the fitted model
and that environment together, then use `envir` when predicting at new
observations:

```{r local-function}
fit_local <- function(dat) {
  shift <- 0.5
  transform_x <- function(x) log(x + shift)
  f <- y ~ s(transform_x(x), k = 6) + offset(log(effort))
  list(model = gam(f, family = poisson(), data = dat, method = "REML"),
    envir = environment(f))
}
bundle <- fit_local(dat)
smooth_estimates(bundle$model, data = nd, envir = bundle$envir)
fitted_values(bundle$model, data = nd, envir = bundle$envir)
```

New predictions require the original definition of `transform_x()` and the
same value of `shift`. Retaining `bundle$envir` makes both available after
`fit_local()` has returned.

## Choose whether derivatives describe change in `x` or `log(x)`

For a contribution $f(\log x)$, the default derivative is with respect to
$\log x$. Set `wrt = "covariate"` to differentiate with respect to $x$ instead.
The latter includes the chain-rule factor $1/x$. We compare both derivatives
at the prediction rows created earlier. Both describe change in the smooth's
contribution to the log expected count; use `response_derivatives()` for change
in the complete response mean.

```{r derivatives}
derivatives(m, data = nd, type = "central")
derivatives(m, data = nd, type = "central", wrt = "covariate")
```

### Differentiate a surface with respect to one covariate

For a surface, `partial_derivatives()` varies the coordinate named in `focal`
while holding the other coordinates fixed. `wrt` chooses the scale of that
coordinate. For example, `te(log(x), sqrt(z))` represents a contribution
$f(\log x, \sqrt z)$, with the following choices:

| Arguments | Derivative |
|:----------|:-----------|
| `wrt = "smooth", focal = "log(x)"` | With respect to $\log x$, holding $\sqrt z$ fixed |
| `wrt = "covariate", focal = "x"` | With respect to $x$, holding $z$ fixed |

We simulate a Gaussian response with mean `sin(log(x)) * sqrt(z)`. The positive
covariates are sampled independently, and independent Gaussian errors have
standard deviation 0.1.

```{r partial-derivatives-data}
set.seed(43)
tensor_dat <- data.frame(x = runif(150, 1, 5), z = runif(150, 1, 3))
tensor_dat$y <- sin(log(tensor_dat$x)) * sqrt(tensor_dat$z) +
  rnorm(nrow(tensor_dat), sd = 0.1)
```

We fit a tensor-product smooth using the transformed covariates to estimate
that surface:

```{r partial-derivatives-model}
tensor_model <- gam(y ~ te(log(x), sqrt(z), k = c(4, 4)),
  data = tensor_dat, method = "REML")
```

Next, we hold `z` at two and vary `x`. We calculate derivatives with respect to
`log(x)` and `x`, then compare the latter with the chain-rule calculation:

```{r partial-derivatives}
# Vary x along a slice with z held fixed.
tensor_nd <- data.frame(x = seq(1.2, 4.8, length.out = 8), z = 2)
pd_smooth <- partial_derivatives(tensor_model, data = tensor_nd,
  wrt = "smooth", focal = "log(x)", type = "central")
pd_covariate <- partial_derivatives(tensor_model, data = tensor_nd,
  wrt = "covariate", focal = "x", type = "central")

# Compare the raw-covariate derivative with the chain-rule calculation.
data.frame(x = tensor_nd$x,
  covariate_derivative = pd_covariate$.partial_deriv,
  smooth_derivative_over_x = pd_smooth$.partial_deriv / tensor_nd$x)
```

The first call estimates the derivative from small changes in `log(x)`. The
second makes small changes in `x` and recalculates `log(x)` before evaluating
the smooth. The chain rule gives the relationship
$\partial f / \partial x = (\partial f / \partial \log x) / x$,
up to finite-difference approximation error.

For this surface, use `focal = "x"` or `"z"` with `wrt = "covariate"`, and
supply the original covariate values in `data`. Keep the other covariate fixed
to describe change along a particular slice, as we did with `z = 2`.
The default `wrt = "smooth"` selects the first numeric smooth coordinate if
`focal` is omitted. Naming it explicitly makes the intended derivative clear.
For an untransformed coordinate, such as `x` in `te(x, z)`, both values of
`wrt` give the same interpretation.

### Choosing a finite-difference step

The derivative functions use `eps = NULL` by default to choose a step from the
fitted range of the differentiation coordinate. This is the range of `log(x)`
when differentiating on that smooth coordinate, or of `x` when using
`wrt = "covariate"`. The step therefore follows changes in the covariate's
units and normally stays the same when prediction data are split into batches.

Start with this default. If estimates appear unstable, supply a positive
absolute `eps` in the units of the coordinate being differentiated. For
example, `eps = 1e-4` with `wrt = "covariate"` sets the step in units of `x`.
Compare estimates using
half and twice the chosen step: very small steps can amplify rounding errors,
while large steps give a poorer local approximation. Near a transformation's
domain boundary, choose a step and difference type that keep the evaluation
points inside the domain. The
[FiniteDiff step-size discussion](https://docs.sciml.ai/FiniteDiff/dev/epsilons/)
explains this balance.
